steps.say: Endocarditis starts with a roughened valve and a passing bacteraemia. Platelets and fibrin settle on the injured endothelium, circulating bacteria lodge in the mesh, and a vegetation grows that sheds septic emboli downstream. Damaged or prosthetic surfaces invite colonisation that healthy valves resist.
steps.tx: **Infective endocarditis** begins when **fibrin and platelets** deposit on injured endothelium and trap **circulating bacteria** into a growing **vegetation**. The mass sheds **septic emboli** while enzymes eat into leaflets, chords, and abscess cavities. Congenital lesions, prosthetic material, and previous infection provide the roughened surfaces that healthy valves lack.

steps.say: Diagnosis follows the modified Duke rules, not impressions. Definitive disease needs 2 major criteria, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Echocardiographic vegetations and persistently positive blood cultures are the two majors that anchor every decision.
steps.tx: The **modified Duke criteria** define definitive disease as **2 major criteria**, **1 major plus 3 minor**, or **5 minor criteria**. **Echocardiography** showing vegetations, abscess, or new dehiscence and **persistently positive blood cultures** are the **major criteria**. Three separate culture sets before antibiotics plus early echo decide most cases within days.

steps.say: Two bacterial families dominate the paediatric ward, seeding damaged valves. Viridans group streptococci such as Streptococcus mitis and oralis seed damaged valves after dental bacteraemia, while Staphylococcus aureus strikes aggressively, including previously normal valves. Culture results steer the weeks of therapy that follow.
steps.tx: The **bacterial pathogens in CHD** are **viridans group streptococci (Streptococcus mitis, oralis)** and **Staphylococcus aureus**, the two predominant organisms in children with **congenital heart disease**. Viridans species follow dental procedures on roughened valves, while aureus runs a destructive course with abscess and emboli. Prior antibiotics blunt cultures, so **three sets before the first dose** remain the rule.

steps.say: Prophylaxis is now reserved for the few at real risk. Antibiotics before procedures go only to prosthetic valves or material, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic disease, repaired disease with residual defects, or children within 6 months of repair. Ordinary murmurs and closed defects earn no prophylaxis.
steps.tx: **Antibiotic prophylaxis** is restricted to **high-risk cardiac lesions**: **prosthetic cardiac valves or material**, **previous infective endocarditis**, **unrepaired cyanotic CHD**, **repaired CHD with residual defects**, or **within 6 months of repair**. Routine VSD, ASD, and PDA closures without residue need none after endothelialisation. Narrow targeting preserves efficacy and limits resistance.

steps.say: Dental work on gum tissue is the classic trigger worth covering. A single oral dose of amoxicillin at 50 milligrams per kilogram up to 2 grams, given 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure, protects high risk children. Only procedures that manipulate gingival tissue or perforate mucosa qualify.
steps.tx: The **dental prophylaxis regimen** is single dose **amoxicillin 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g)** given **30-60 minutes before** invasive **dental procedures manipulating gingival tissue** protects high risk children. The single dose beats prolonged courses for compliance and ecology. Cleanings without bleeding, fillings above the gum line, and lip injuries need no cover.

steps.say: Allergy changes the drug while sparing the principle. With severe immediate type penicillin allergy, cephalexin at 50 milligrams per kilogram, azithromycin at 15 milligrams per kilogram, or clarithromycin at 15 milligrams per kilogram, replacing amoxicillin. The single dose timing before the procedure stays exactly the same.
steps.tx: **Penicillin allergy alternatives** for severe **immediate type penicillin allergy**, **cephalexin (50 mg/kg)**, **azithromycin (15 mg/kg)**, or **clarithromycin (15 mg/kg)**, replacing amoxicillin as a **single pre procedure dose**. Macrolides suit children who cannot take beta lactams at all. Documenting the allergy phenotype avoids both anaphylaxis and unnecessarily broad cover.

steps.say: Once infection is established, treatment is measured in weeks of intravenous drugs. Native valve disease starts on ampicillin at 200 milligrams per kilogram per day or ceftriaxone with gentamicin at 3 milligrams per kilogram per day, adding vancomycin when methicillin resistant aureus is suspected. Doses split across the day keep levels above the kill threshold.
steps.tx: **Empiric antimicrobial therapy** for **native valve** disease combines **ampicillin (200 mg/kg/day)** or **ceftriaxone** with **gentamicin (3 mg/kg/day)**, adding **vancomycin** if **methicillin resistant S. aureus** is suspected. Therapy narrows once cultures and sensitivities return. Four to six weeks of parenteral treatment with drug level and renal monitoring cures most uncomplicated cases.

steps.say: Surgery rescues valves that drugs cannot save, acting before the next embolus lands. Persistent vegetation above 10 millimetres with embolic events, severe valvular regurgitation driving refractory heart failure, or a perivalvular abscess each earns valve repair or replacement. Operating before the next embolus lands is the whole point.
steps.tx: The **vegetation size indications for surgery** are persistent **vegetation above 10 mm with embolic events**, so **surgical valve repair or replacement** is indicated, severe **valvular regurgitation with refractory heart failure**, or **perivalvular abscess**. Heart block from septal abscess and dehisced prostheses join the list. Timing weighs sterilisation against destruction, and the endocarditis team decides together.

nodes.label: Large embolic vegetation or abscess found
Heart failure or conduction injury follows

steps.say: Textbook skin signs are rarer in children than examinations suggest. Classic immunological and vascular stigmata such as Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, and splinter haemorrhages appear in under 10 to 15 percent of paediatric cases. Their absence never excludes the disease, but their presence should accelerate the workup.
steps.tx: **Peripheral stigmata rarity** marks paediatric disease: classic **immunological and vascular stigmata (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages)** are present in **under 10-15%** of children with infective endocarditis. Paediatric disease moves too fast for many signs to develop. Examine the fundi, fingers, and toes in every suspected case, but trust cultures and echo over skin.
